Day 3 · Biggest insightThey already called two other firms before yoursPreheader: What a scared caller does before they pick.

Hi *|IF:MMERGE19||MMERGE19||ELSE:|*there*|END:IF|*,

Here's the part of the 40% Problem report worth sitting with for a second.

Someone gets arrested, or served, or told their marriage is over. They are scared, and they don't call one lawyer. They call three, sometimes at 11pm from a parking lot, and they hire whoever calls back first and sounds like they know what to do next.

That's the real insight behind the 40% number. It was never "does my firm do good work." It's "when someone is deciding in a panic, does my firm even answer?" Six in ten firms don't answer at all, and almost half never answer or call back, period.

A firm that's easy to find online and quick to respond wins that moment before the first meeting ever happens. A firm that's slow, or invisible online in the first place, loses it and never even finds out the person existed.

That moment is what the law firm program is built around.

Day 5 · Objection: price$750 a month, or a $16.73 click that goes nowhere?Preheader: The math, done the honest way.

Hi *|IF:MMERGE19||MMERGE19||ELSE:|*there*|END:IF|*,

Let me guess what's giving you pause. The number.

Fair. So let's do the math the way a firm actually pays for clients.

A Google click on "criminal defense lawyer near me" runs about $16.73, and only around 7 in 100 legal ad clicks turn into an inquiry at all. That works out to roughly $239 for every person who reaches out, before your close rate, which for paid search typically runs 8% to 15%. Run that math and one new client from Google Ads costs somewhere around $1,400 to $3,000. The Spark Sites Law Firm Program is $4,500 to set up, then $0 a month until your first new-client inquiry, then $750 a month after that, month to month.

A first-offense DUI in Florida runs $2,500 to $7,500, averaging around $3,500. One client covers the setup fee. Everything after that is a system you own instead of ad spend you pay every month whether it converts or not.

The site isn't the cost. The callers who found someone else first are the cost.

Day 7 · Objection: referrals/directoriesWhy I don't worry about AvvoPreheader: You can rent a spot on a directory. Here's what happens when you do.

Hi *|IF:MMERGE19||MMERGE19||ELSE:|*there*|END:IF|*,

You can pay for a spot on Avvo, Martindale, FindLaw, or the next directory that calls. It works, sort of, and plenty of firms run mostly on referrals and never touch any of this. I'd never pretend either one is wrong.

Here's what I've seen happen to firms that lean entirely on one or the other.

Avvo's paid tiers start around $49 to $100 a month, and some firms report spending close to $14,000 a year once everything is added up. One Connecticut firm sued Thomson Reuters after paying more than $28,000 on a $2,336-a-month FindLaw contract and never getting the website it was promised. Referrals, meanwhile, dry up the moment your best referring clients stop needing a lawyer for a while. Either way, you never owned the thing bringing you the next client.

A website that ranks for your practice areas, a Google Business Profile that shows up in the map pack, and reviews that keep landing don't shut off when a referral source goes quiet or a directory bill comes due. They compound, month over month, and they're yours.

The law firm program builds the thing you own, right alongside whatever referrals keep coming. Just don't build your whole intake on something you're renting or hoping for.

Day 14 · Usable tipCall your own office at 12:15 todayPreheader: Free, five minutes, and you'll know exactly where you stand.

Hi *|IF:MMERGE19||MMERGE19||ELSE:|*there*|END:IF|*,

No pitch today, just something you can do this afternoon whether you ever talk to us again or not.

Call your own firm at 12:15, from a phone your staff won't recognize. Call again at 5:45. Then fill out your own website's contact form at 9pm. Write down what actually happens each time: does it ring through, does anyone call back, how long does it take.

That's the exact test a research firm ran on 500 law firms in 2024. Only 40% answered the phone. 48% never answered or called back at all. Only 33% replied to an email inquiry. Whatever you find on your own firm this afternoon is what every scared caller experiences before they ever meet you.

Day 21 · Usable tipThe one line every consultation page is missingPreheader: Small change, big difference.

Hi *|IF:MMERGE19||MMERGE19||ELSE:|*there*|END:IF|*,

Here's a free one worth more than most paid advice.

The biggest reason a law firm site doesn't generate calls usually isn't the design. It's that it never tells the visitor what happens next, and it doesn't work at 11pm when someone's sitting in a parking lot on their phone.

"Schedule your free consultation," one clear instruction, repeated on every practice-area page, plus a phone number that's tappable on mobile without hunting for it. Legal problems don't wait for business hours. The firm that's one tap away gets the call. The one with "Contact Us" buried in a footer menu gets scrolled past.

Look at your own site with that lens. You'll never unsee it. Making that instruction impossible to miss, on every page, is half of what we build.

Day 24 · Industry insightThe three law firms your neighbors actually seePreheader: The map pack, and why you might not be in it.

Hi *|IF:MMERGE19||MMERGE19||ELSE:|*there*|END:IF|*,

Quick insight, because it changes how you think about all of this.

When someone near you searches "divorce lawyer near me" or "DUI lawyer near me," Google doesn't show them the whole internet. It shows a short local list, usually three firms, above everything else. That list is where the calls come from.

You get into that list with a complete Google Business Profile (every practice area listed as its own service, your counties as your service area) tied to a website with a dedicated page per practice area, and reviews landing every month. When we did exactly that for Superior Spray here in Central Florida, their search traffic climbed 276% and leads started finding them without a single rented lead. Firms without that setup mostly don't show up, no matter how good the casework is. Being great and being invisible look identical to someone searching from their phone.

It's not about beating every firm in the state. It's about being one of the three names your own county sees. That's exactly what the law firm program builds toward.

Day 35 · Industry insightThe mistake I see on most law firm websitesPreheader: It's costing them calls right now.

Hi *|IF:MMERGE19||MMERGE19||ELSE:|*there*|END:IF|*,

Last insight in this batch, and it's the most common one.

Most law firm sites I look at are built to talk about the firm: years in practice, a photo of the building, generic credibility language. The Florida Bar rightly keeps anyone from calling themselves an "expert" or a "specialist" without board certification, so a lot of firms lean even harder on that same generic language instead of saying anything useful.

The person reading it has one question: "I was just arrested for a DUI, what happens to me now?" or "My spouse just filed, what do I do first?" The sites that get the call answer that question, in plain language, with a next step at the end, not a slogan.

Read your own site's first paragraph. Is it about the firm, or about the person who's scared and searching at midnight? That one shift changes everything, and it's the lens we build every practice-area page through.
